title: Back then
job: Habits and states in the past; then against now
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE IMPERFECT ARRIVES, THIRTY-FOUR MODULES AFTER L1-M5 DEFERRED IT. That module settled that the past in this course was the perfect and only the perfect, and named THREE KEYS to hold open for exactly this rung: legēbam, habēbam and eram. Every review doc from docs/126 to docs/132 confirmed they were still free. All three are spent here. The -bam ending is a habit or a state that went ON; the perfect is a single finished event — and the whole course has been living without the distinction long enough for it to be felt rather than explained.

eram IS THE ONE L1-M5 COULD NOT GIVE YOU, AND YOU HAVE BEEN NEEDING IT SINCE L1-M9. fuī was 'I was' as an event and eram is 'I was' as a state, and every module from L1-M9 to L3-M10 used fuī where English would have said eram: sollicitus fuī, aeger fuī, fessus fuī. Those sentences were not wrong — they treated a state as an event because there was nothing else — and this module is where they can finally be said the other way.

THE LOCATIVE IS WRITTEN HERE AND M9 EXPLAINS IT. Rōmae is 'at Rome' with no preposition, and a habit needs a place — so this module borrows the shape exactly as M6 borrowed the imperfect, and says so in every note. M9 is where city names and home are taught as a closed list.

ALL THREE RESERVED KEYS ARE IN THIS MODULE's FIRST FOUR SENTENCES, and nunc arrives with the third. Thirty-four modules have managed without a word for 'now' because the present tense carried it — and ōlim against nunc is the job of this module in one line: the imperfect holds the stretch that is over, the present holds the one that is not.

sōlēbam IS THE TENSE SAYING ITS OWN NAME: the imperfect of soleō, 'I am accustomed', plus an INFINITIVE. sōlēbam legere and legēbam mean nearly the same thing, and sōlēbam is the gentler way in for an English speaker while the plain imperfect is what a Roman wrote. Its plate is sōlēbam legēbam — the imperfect after a word that already is one, which is the commonest slip once a learner has both shapes.

habitārem IS A MOOD AND habitābam IS A TENSE, AND THEY ARE ONE LETTER APART. M3 opened the imperfect SUBJUNCTIVE for present unreal conditions and M6 used it for time clauses; this module owns the imperfect INDICATIVE. Both those modules' notes disown this one's shape and this one disowns theirs — which is the arrangement docs/131 §2.1 set up four modules in advance, and S06 is the sentence that shows why it was needed.

'I used to live' — the imperfect of habitō, 'I live, I dwell', with habitāre as its infinitive. The -bam ending is the tense, and English 'inhabit' keeps the verb.

words.note: 'Once, back then'. It takes no ending and it marks a stretch of past time rather than a moment — which is what the imperfect is for.

'I used to have' — the imperfect of habeō, and the third of L1-M5's reserved keys. All three are now spent, in this module's first four sentences.
'Now'. Thirty-four modules have managed without it, because the present tense carried it. Here it is, for the sake of the contrast with ōlim.
'Not', in front of what it denies.
'I have': habeō, habēs, habet. L1-M1's verb, and its present has been in the course from the first module.

'Every day'. L1-M4's word.

sentences.display: Ōlim medicum nōn habēbam; nunc habeō.
sentences.cue: Back then I did not have a doctor; now I do.
sentences.literal: once doctor not I-was-having now I-have

words.note: 'Once, back then'. It takes no ending and it marks a stretch of past time rather than a moment — which is what the imperfect is for.
'Doctor' as the object. L3-M7's word.
'Not', in front of what it denies.
'I used to have' — the imperfect of habeō, and one of L1-M5's three reserved keys.
'Now'. Thirty-four modules have managed without it, because the present tense carried it. Here it is, for the sake of the contrast with ōlim.
'I have': habeō, habēs, habet. L1-M1's verb.

sentences.trap: The second half has no object and needs none. Latin drops what a reader can supply — L4-M7's signs did the same with est — so nunc habeō is 'now I do have one', with the doctor understood from four words earlier.

sentences.display: Ōlim Rōmae habitābam; nunc hīc habitō et gaudeō.
sentences.cue: I used to live in Rome; now I live here and I am glad.
sentences.literal: once at-Rome I-was-living now here I-live and I-am-glad

words.note: 'Once, back then'. It takes no ending and it marks a stretch of past time rather than a moment — which is what the imperfect is for.
'At Rome' — the locative, which M9 explains.
'I used to live' — the imperfect of habitō.
'Now'. Thirty-four modules have managed without it, because the present tense carried it. Here it is, for the sake of the contrast with ōlim.
'Here'. L1-M7's word.
'I live, I dwell': habitō, habitat. The present of the verb whose imperfect opens this module.
'And'. L1-M1's word.
'I am glad': gaudeō, gaudet. M3's verb.

sentences.trap: Two tenses and one sentence, and neither is doing the other's job. The imperfect holds the stretch that is over and the present holds the one that is not — which is exactly the division English makes with 'used to live' and 'live', and which this course could not make at all until this module.

sentences.display: Sōlēbam aeger esse; nunc nōn sum.
sentences.cue: I used to be ill; now I am not.
sentences.literal: I-was-accustomed ill to-be now not I-am

words.note: 'I used to' — the imperfect of soleō, 'I am accustomed'. It takes an infinitive, and it is the tense saying its own name.
'Ill' — aeger, aegra, aegrum, agreeing with the speaker.
'To be' — sum's infinitive, and the shape sōlēbam needs. L3-M3's word.
'Now'. Thirty-four modules have managed without it, because the present tense carried it. Here it is, for the sake of the contrast with ōlim.
'Not', in front of what it denies.
'I am' — sum, es, est, sunt. L1-M1's verb.

sentences.trap: sōlēbam aeger esse and ōlim aeger eram say nearly the same thing, and the difference is that sōlēbam insists on the habit. Being ill is not usually a habit, which is why this sentence reads as mildly odd in Latin exactly as 'I used to be ill' does in English — and that is the honest limit of the construction.

sentences.display: Cum Rōmae habitārem, tempus habēbam et cotīdiē legēbam; nunc nōn legō.
sentences.cue: When I was living in Rome, I had time and read every day; now I do not read.
sentences.literal: when at-Rome I-was-living time I-was-having and daily I-was-reading now not I-read

words.note: 'When' with a subjunctive — M6's reading. A case after cum means 'with'.
'At Rome' — the locative, which M9 explains.
'When I was living' — the imperfect SUBJUNCTIVE, which cum requires. One letter from habitābam.
'Time' — neuter, so it looks the same as a subject and as an object.
'I used to have' — the imperfect of habeō, one of L1-M5's three reserved keys.
'And'. L1-M1's word, joining two imperfects.
'Every day'. L1-M4's word.
'I was reading, I used to read' — the imperfect of legō. L1-M5 named this key thirty-four modules ago and forbade every module since to write it.
'Now'. Thirty-four modules have managed without it, because the present tense carried it. Here it is, for the sake of the contrast with ōlim.
'Not', in front of what it denies.
'I read': legō, legis, legit, legimus. L1-M4's verb.

sentences.trap: All three of L1-M5's reserved keys are in this module, and two of them are in this sentence. Thirty-four modules of writing the perfect because there was nothing else, and now a stretch of past time can be held open for as long as the sentence needs — which is what the whole deferral was for.
sentences.sound: cum RŌ-mae ha-bi-TĀ-rem, TEM-pus ha-BĒ-bam et co-tī-di-Ē le-GĒ-bam; NUNC nōn LE-gō. Twenty-five syllables — the longest line of the module.

mistake.display: Cum Rōmae habitārem, tempus habuī et cotīdiē lēgī.
mistake.why: two perfects for two habits. It is the shape thirty-four modules have trained, and in this sentence it says the having and the reading each happened once — which is the exact thing the imperfect was held back to be able to correct.
